summary:
Artemis Quest is a free 3D cartoon game for children aged 7 to 12. It runs in the browser, with no download and no account. Players command a base in Jezero Crater on Mars, or near Shackleton Crater at the Moon's south pole, for 15 sols (Martian days). Each sol, they split a limited supply of solar energy between life support, radiation shielding and science. Whatever is left charges the battery for the night.

Every choice has a cost. Shielding takes energy away from science, and skipping it leaves the crew exposed to solar storms. Playing it safe keeps everyone alive, but without discoveries the mission earns only one star. Each match replays a real historical window. Its solar storms come from NASA's DONKI records, and messages from Earth arrive with the real delay calculated by JPL Horizons for that day. Guided tutorials, events that change every match and an online co-op mode for classrooms make it easy to play again.

This matters because children rarely see the reasoning behind a space mission. They usually see only the result. In Artemis Quest they feel real engineering trade-offs themselves, using real NASA data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Artemis Quest is a 3D cartoon management game that runs in the browser. Children aged 7 to 12 command a base for 15 sols (Martian days), in Jezero Crater on Mars or near Shackleton Crater at the Moon's south pole. One match takes about 10 to 15 minutes.

Each sol, the solar panels produce a few blocks of energy. The player splits them between three core resources by tapping places in the 3D base:

- Life support (air, water, food) at the greenhouse.

- Radiation shielding at the shelter, where robots dig regolith into bags for the shelter.

- Science: the rover goes on an expedition and fills real sample tubes. Perseverance carried 38 tubes, so tubes are scarce too.

Unused energy charges the battery, and the night uses it up. Before the player ends the sol, a preview shows the result ("Life: 70 -> 76"). After it, a report explains cause and effect.

Real NASA data drives the risk:

- DONKI: each match replays one of 6 real 15-sol windows from 2023 to 2025, with the real solar storms (CMEs) of that period.

- JPL Horizons: messages from Earth arrive with the real Earth-Mars delay for that day (3 to 22 minutes). Earth warns the crew one sol before a storm hits.

- NASA image library: real photos (Apollo, Viking) appear during the trip intro.

The game always says this data was downloaded, never "live." The radiation dose is labeled as a game scale, not real mSv.

Winning: surviving all 15 sols earns 1 star. Surviving with 100 science earns 2 stars, and doing it with a low radiation dose earns 3. We tested 2,000 simulated matches per strategy. "Science only" always fails, "safety only" always gets 1 star, and only a player who reacts to warnings and keeps a reserve wins well. No choice is free.

BENEFITS

- No barrier to entry: it runs in the browser, needs no download or account, and works on desktop and phone. It can be installed as an app (PWA), and solo mode works offline after the first visit.

- Learning by playing: the first 3 sols are a guided tutorial, so there is no manual to read. Every text has at most 2 sentences of 8 to 12 words. Science terms get a simple explanation in context, like "sol (Mars day)".

- Replay value: every match has a different historical window, a random dust storm and 4 of 8 decision cards. Losing is not punishing: the end screen explains what happened and offers a new mission.

- Three difficulty levels (ages 7+, 9+, 11+): only the game scale changes. The real NASA data stays the same at every level, and an automated test checks this.

- Classroom co-op: 2 to 5 players join online, each on their own device. One player is Mission Control on Earth and can only send delayed messages. The others are Commander, Flight Engineer, Medical Officer and Scientist, the same crew roles as NASA's CHAPEA analog, and they share one energy budget.

INTENDED IMPACT

Space content for children is usually either too abstract or too technical. Children see a mission's result, almost never the reasoning behind it. We want each child to finish a match able to explain four real constraints in their own words:

1. Energy is limited, and the night charges for it.

2. Protection costs a lot, but having none can end the mission.

3. Earth is far away, so sometimes the crew must decide alone.

4. Playing only safe also fails, because the mission exists to do science.

Teachers and parents get documentation with every data source, so they can lead a conversation after the game.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

- Game client: TypeScript, Three.js (toon shading with ink outlines), Vite, Rapier physics (loaded only on demand).

- Game rules: a pure TypeScript simulation with no rendering code, tested with Node's test runner and a balance script that plays 2,000 matches per strategy.

- Co-op server: Go, running the same TypeScript rules through the embedded goja JavaScript engine, so the rules live in one place only.

- Data: Node scripts that download DONKI (NASA Open APIs) and JPL Horizons data into curated JSON files.

- Deployment: GitHub Pages for the game, Docker and Cloudflare Tunnel for the co-op server, PWA through vite-plugin-pwa.

- Process: Git and GitHub pull requests with review, Architecture Decision Records (15 ADRs), and AI-assisted coding with Claude Code.

- Hardware: none needed. Any browser on a computer or phone works.

CREATIVITY

- Shielding is mass, not magic. Energy powers machines that dig regolith into bags for the shelter. This is based on NASA's RASSOR excavator and the way Orion crews build a shelter from stowage bags.

- You replay real history: "this storm really happened on this date," with the real communication delay for that day.

- Co-op that teaches through its structure. Earth sees space weather before the crew does but can't decide. Mars decides but gets warnings late. Each side needs the other.

- A scientifically accurate base: modules use NASA measurements, crew quarters are private rooms, and the rover never goes to a garage. It sleeps wherever it is, like Perseverance.

- Two worlds with different lessons. On the Moon there are no dust storms. The challenge there is mountains blocking the Sun, and messages take about 1 second.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age 7 to 12 first: when "richer" conflicts with "simpler for the child," simpler wins. We follow a written language guide, icons always come with text, color is never the only signal, buttons are big, and controls work with screen readers and keyboards.

- Data honesty: every in-game fact has a recorded official source. Real data, game-scale values and predictions are always clearly labeled.

- The challenge's pitfalls: only 3 core resources, no "safe" choice without a cost, and mechanics checked by simulation, not just visuals.

- Children's privacy: the co-op server stores no names, accounts or personal data.

- Maintainability for a small team: rules in one place, a single file for all game numbers, and documentation updated in the same pull request as the code.
